activity.text: HCPs have stopped searching and started asking. When a physician brings a clinical question to an AI instead of a search bar, your brand is either in the answer they get back or it isn't. That's a different game than the one most commercial teams are set up to play. On July 29 I'm joining a Fierce Pharma webinar to get into what that actually means for pharma commercial: "Driving Share of Answer Through Optichannel Engagement in the AI Era." I'll be with Dana Cohen and Brian Bieniowski digging into how teams hold visibility when the point of decision has moved inside an AI answer. Some of what we'll cover: - Why optimizing for clicks and Share of Voice stops working once the citation in the AI answer is the thing that matters. - How to get your AI, digital, and field efforts pointing at the same HCP instead of working past each other. - What KPIs even mean when physicians are skipping search entirely, and how to set a baseline now that your 2027 brand plan can actually build on. This is aimed at anyone weighing expensive AI media buys or trying to earn organic citations the harder way. Register here: https://lnkd.in/ghCUCEXQ

Reps are still walking into clinics without a full picture, with target lists from last quarter, while live digital signals live in a black box. That is a glaring data latency problem in most pharma tech stacks. We asked 151 execs what is actually blocking their data from driving real field decisions. Here is the reality: • 62% say data fragmentation limits their visibility. • 61% are dealing with lagging information trapped across disconnected systems. • 51% admit their predictive analytics just aren't where they need to be. • 43% cannot link digital or field touchpoints back to script lift. While marketing is busy tracking real-world data in the digital world, sales is often left in a vacuum. Reps end up burning time on low-intent visits and missing high-value opportunities. It is no surprise that 53% of sales teams are actively asking for better targeting guidance, and 46% want a clear window into digital customer behavior. A predictive Next-Best-Action (NBA) engine can bridge this gap by putting live direction right into the rep's existing CRM workflow. But let's be candid: dropping raw, unexplained alerts into a CRM doesn't work. Reps naturally ignore "black box" algorithms they don't understand or trust. If you want the field to adopt the strategy, you have to give them the why: "Dr. Smith opened our clinical efficacy email 12 hours ago and shows a high affinity for mechanism of action (MOA) content." Giving reps that explicit context drives an immediate 22% jump in brand strategy adherence. The full, closed loop should look like this: 1. Capture live digital signals. 2. Personalize the HCP journey on their preferred channels. 3. Trigger a transparent CRM nudge. 4. Give the field force the full context. 5. Measure and attribute real script lift. Where does this loop usually break down for your team, unifying data sources upfront, providing transparency to reps, or handling real-time script attribution at the end?

Most Pharma AI evaluations ask "what can this tool do?" when the more useful question is "does this tool understand what we do?" This is a clip from my Fierce Pharma interview on what I think actually matters when life sciences leaders are evaluating AI tools. The three criteria map to the same operating-model thesis I've been writing about, just applied to the build/buy decision: 1) Industry context. Does the tool understand pharma's data, regulations, and decision rules? The gap between "powerful" and "compliant in pharma" is wider than most evaluation frameworks acknowledge. 2) Transparency and traceability. Can you trace how the tool got to its recommendation? For anything that shapes content influencing prescribing, you need the audit trail to defend: to MLR, regulatory, and increasingly the AI governance function. 3) Adoption alignment. AI value is locked behind use. The brilliant pilot that nobody actually uses is the most common failure mode I see. AI works when the tool, the team, and the source of truth are designed together.

I wrote an article on the growing AI Judgment Gap afew weeks ago: the gap between work produced with AI assistance and our understanding and ownership of it. This follow up is about how judgment has structure. When someone reviews a piece of AI-assisted work, they often checking the same few things (whether they can explain what's being claimed, whether they verified what might otherwise be taken on faith, and whether their confidence matches their grasp). Once we make that structure explicit, then we can score it. I call that score AI-Q: a measure from 0 to 100 considering: Discernment, Delegation, Design. Ultimately it translates into four bands, from "Owns it" (you could defend this in front of anyone) down to "Black box" (you shipped something you don't yet understand). If AI evals measure models, AI-Q measures us. Hone is a tool that runs this assessment. In five minutes you can score any piece of AI-assisted work, measure an AI-Q score, and understand which dimensions to develop to ensure that as we use AI, we are not atrophying judgment. Let me know if you want to try it out. What band would your last AI-assisted work product land in? #AI #Leadership #Judgment #AIQ

Really enjoyed this panel session at NEXT Pharma Summit and the discussions there. It really highlighted that the old playbook is not going to prepare us for what is coming next with Share of Answer. Share of Voice assumed being seen led to being chosen. But when physicians are asking AI clinical questions directly, what decides outcomes is whether your brand is in the answer they get back. What I proposed at NEXT is that this isn't a new channel to bolt onto the media plan. It's a new unit of competition that Pharma operating models still haven’t adapted to because the team that owns the evidence is now the team that owns the answer.

Share of Answer isn't just a marketing problem. That was the takeaway from an operating-model piece I wrote a few weeks ago. The question I got most often was: "so what does that actually mean for my function?" So these are my thoughts on the answer, function by function. The brands winning Share of Answer aren't the ones with the best websites. They're the ones whose evidence is densely cited across the sources AI engines actually pull from, and that kind of citation density is not something any single team can build on its own. Brand can't get there without medical, and medical can't get there without regulatory behind it. The article walks through what each team has to build differently. - For brand and commercial, the metric shifts from Share of Voice to Share of Answer, and the thing you've optimized for a decade quietly stops mattering. - For medical affairs, the job moves from explaining the evidence to engineering the source the machines paraphrase from. - Regulatory and MLR shift from gatekeeping your own pages to monitoring what AI says about your brand on surfaces you don't control. - And on the HCP and patient journey, the hard part is what happens when the first touchpoint is an AI the brand never sees. But the most important part is the connective tissue across each. They all converge on one artifact: a governed, machine-readable source of truth that every AI surface can be pointed at. Your approved claims sit on one layer, the questions HCPs actually ask sit on another, and the two are mapped to each other, with brand, medical, and MLR all signing off on the same versioned thing instead of trading redlines in Word. In my working thesis, I propose it should be designed using Google's Open Knowledge Format, and be brand-owned and portable (instead of locked inside whichever agency built your structured layer last). That's the artifact none of the functions can produce alone, and it's the one that ends up deciding whether the machine cites you or your competitor. I'd love to know where you think your own function lands in this. #ShareOfAnswer #Pharma #AI

I added an album to my radio app for the Summer. My son just wrapped up kindergarten and his social life has gotten predictably complicated: Kids choosing favorites at recess, the friend he played with yesterday playing with someone else today, and learning when to walk away and when to try again. The album is called "The Summer We Grew Up". The tracks are named like the parenting moments that inspired them: Not Everything's a Race, Can I Play Too, Bad Day Good Tomorrow, Different Than I Planned, Everybody's Good At Something. Making this also helped me articulate an important consideration in making AI impactful. AI requires context, and context is not one artifact. It's a coherent body of artifacts that build on each other. One well-shaped song teaches a feeling but an album teaches a curriculum. A kid hearing eight songs together then starts to internalize the themes, not just the individual skills or lessons. The same is true with AI visibility in Pharma or any industry. One well-shaped piece of content doesn't move Share of Answer. A centralized, coherent, and well structured body of context does. Models needs a body of context that says the same thing in different shapes, to triangulate on what your brand actually means, not what one piece of collateral says about it. This is the potential value of Google's Open Knowledge Format (OKF) if used in the right way for this use case. Album link in first comment. If you have a kid 4–9 and a summer to fill, have a listen.

🚸The front door to healthcare might not just be a clinic — it might also be an AI prompt.🚸 The number one search topic on Microsoft Copilot every month of 2025 was health, and that is not a temporary spike but a sustained shift in behavior. It is also not isolated. OpenAI reports that of its 900 million weekly active users on ChatGPT , one in four engages with health-related questions every week. So what are people actually searching for? This Microsoft AI report ( https://lnkd.in/eRxdmRaq ) shows that people are not just looking for wellness advice. They are looking for interpretation and guidance on their health concerns. They want to understand symptoms, make sense of results, and know what to do next. This is deeply personal decision-making, and it is increasingly happening outside the traditional healthcare system. AI is quickly becoming a complementary front door to health. That raises the stakes and means trust, accuracy, and responsibility become foundational. >>> Join the discussion: 🌱 If AI is becoming the first place people turn for health guidance, how should healthcare leaders respond? #AIinHealthcare #DigitalHealth #HealthAI #PatientExperience #FutureOfCare
